newsitem.title: USA: Clinton, Republicans squabble over deficit credit.
newsitem.headline: Clinton, Republicans squabble over deficit credit.

text.p: President Bill Clinton on Monday claimed election-year credit for new figures showing a further decline in the U.S. budget deficit, saying it was evidence his economic policies were working.

"My fellow Americans, four years ago, I said if you gave us a chance we'd cut that deficit in half to get interest rates down and get the economy going again. It's been cut by 63 percent in four years," Clinton said to lusty applause at a campaign rally here.

The decline in the deficit to $107 billion this year also gave Clinton the opportunity for a rare direct response to Republican challenger Bob Dole's appeal to Americans to "wake up" and reject Clinton in the Nov. 5 election because of a raft of ethical problems.

"My friends, America has heard a lot of calls in the last several days," he told a rally earlier in the St. Louis suburb of University City. "I would say that these results prove that America is awake and moving in the right direction."
White House spokesman Mike McCurry took a harder shot at Dole, saying his drumbeat of attacks showed he was "flailing."
"It's increasingly becoming less necessary to respond as the shrillness and the absurdity of the remarks accelerates."

Republicans contended Clinton deserved no credit on the deficit because they had to drag him into making reductions in government spending after they took control of Congress two years ago. Senate Budget Committee Chairman Pete Domenici of New Mexico said the lower deficit "vindicates our willingness to stand up to Bill Clinton."
Republican National Committee Chairman Haley Barbour pointed out Clinton had proposed a budget for fiscal 1996 predicting deficit spending in excess of $200 billion a year for the foreseeable future.
Analysts said both Democrats and Republicans had helped to reduce the deficit with various actions raising taxes and cutting spending over the last six years.

"I would pat both parties and both branches of government on the back for these numbers," said Robert Reischauer, a senior fellow at the Brookings Institution in Washington and former head of the Congressional Budget Office.
He said both presidents Clinton and George Bush had pushed through deficit-reduction packages that included tax hikes.

Budget analyst Stan Collender of the Burson-Marsteller public relations firm said "if you divide the credit between Clinton and Congress, I would say about 75 percent goes to Clinton and about 25 percent to Congress."
"Remember Clinton got Congress to pass in 1993 a deficit reduction plan, with no Republican votes," Collender said.
Clinton staked claim to the credit for himself on his visit to the "Show Me" state, nicknamed for Missourians' reputation for requiring proof of claims.

On the steps of University City's city hall he stood in front of a large chart showing the country's red-ink spending was $290 billion in 1992 when he was elected and had declined every year he had been in office.

Two teens joined him on stage to pull a string unveiling a deficit figure for the 1996 budget year that ends Oct. 31 of $107 billion, the lowest budget deficit in 15 years, since 1981, Republican Ronald Reagan's first year as president.

If not for deficit-spending under Reagan and his Republican successor George Bush, he asserted, the budget would be in surplus. "We all know that our budget would be in surplus today if it weren't for the interest we pay on the debt rung up in the 12 years before I took office," he said.

Franklin Raines, director of the White House Office of Management and Budget (OMB), which compiles the figure, said the drop reflected both stronger-than-expected growth that raised tax revenue and efforts to control government spending.

Speaking to a crowd of about 10,000 in Minneapolis, Clinton continued turning his attention to boosting Democrats in their effort to oust Republicans from control of Congress. Leading Dole by a large margin in Minnesota, Clinton got in a big plug for Democratic Sen. Paul Wellstone, who is leading in his battle against former Republican Sen. Rudy Boschwitz.
On a three-day, seven-state swing, Clinton was to address another rally in Chicago on Monday night before heading to Columbus, Ohio.
